concept.line: A verb's ending says who does it: radim (I work), radiš (you work), radi (she works), radimo (we work), rade (they work).

Bosnian usually leaves out a subject pronoun when the verb or context identifies it, and it uses no dummy word for the it in “It’s raining” or the there in “There’s no milk”: Radim (I-work), Pada kiša (falls rain: it’s raining).

words.means: je = is; si = you are; jesi = you are; nisam = I am not

concept.line: biti has short forms sam, si, je, smo, ste, and su; its negative forms include nisam (I am not), nisi (you are not), and nije (he, she, or it is not).

words.means: imam = I have; imaš = you have

concept.line: Every noun is masculine (stol), feminine (torba) or neuter (mlijeko), mostly told by its ending, and the words with it match: moj stol, moja torba, moje mlijeko.

words.means: govoriš = you speak; govorim = I speak

concept.line: What a verb acts on takes the accusative, which changes feminine -a to -u (Pijem kahvu: I-drink coffee); u or na + accusative is where you go: Idem u pekaru (I-go into bakery).
